passages.happening:
‘These were the sons of Reuben the firstborn of Israel’ (verse 1). Though he was the firstborn, ‘his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph son of Israel, because Reuben defiled his father’s bed’ (verse 1). ‘And though Judah prevailed over his brothers and a ruler came from him, the birthright belonged to Joseph’ (verse 2).

Reuben's descendants follow, down to a leader carried off by Tiglath-pileser of Assyria, and their lands east of the Jordan (verses 3-10). Then come the families of Gad in Bashan and Gilead, registered in the days of Jotham of Judah and Jeroboam of Israel (verses 11-17).
passages.hearers:
The Chronicler crosses the Jordan to the east. Reuben was Jacob's firstborn and would normally come first, so the chapter explains why he does not. The birthright, usually a double share of inheritance and the leadership of the family, went to Joseph's sons, and leadership came through Judah. Honor and inheritance could be separated. Reuben's act, told in Genesis, was not only a sexual sin but a bid to take his father's place.

Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh settled on the plateau and pasture lands east of the Jordan after Moses defeated Sihon and Og. Several towns named here, Aroer, Nebo and Baal-meon among them, also appear on the Moabite Stone, set up by Mesha king of Moab about 840 BC, which tells of his fighting with Israel in this very region. The eastern tribes lived on a frontier, open to Moab, Aram and the desert peoples.
passages.later: Jacob had said to Reuben, ‘you will no longer excel, because you went up to your father’s bed’ (Genesis 49:4).
passages.asks: Reuben was first by birth and lost his place by what he did. Ask what in your life you have treated as yours by right. And ask what it would mean to hold your place as a gift rather than a claim.

passages.t: Trust in battle, and unfaithfulness that ended in exile
passages.happening:
The eastern tribes, with 44,760 fighting men, go to war against the Hagrites and their allies (verses 18-19). ‘And because they cried out to God in battle, they were helped against their enemies, and the Hagrites and all their allies were delivered into their hands. Because they put their trust in God, He answered their prayers’ (verse 20). They take great herds and many captives, ‘because the battle belonged to God. And they occupied the land until the exile’ (verse 22).

The half-tribe of Manasseh spreads north toward Mount Hermon (verses 23-24). ‘But they were unfaithful to the God of their fathers’ (verse 25), turning to the gods of the peoples of the land. ‘So the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria (that is, Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria) to take the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh into exile’ (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
These two short stories set out the pattern that governs the whole book: seeking God brings help, and unfaithfulness brings exile. They mirror each other. In one the tribes trust God and he gives them their enemies' land; in the other they are unfaithful and he gives them to their enemies. The word for trust, batach, is the Psalms' word for confidence in God rather than in horses or princes. The word for unfaithful, ma'al, is the book's main word for the sin that leads to disaster.

Tiglath-pileser III ruled Assyria about 745 to 727 BC and is also called Pul. Around 733 to 732 BC he took Gilead and Galilee and deported their people. The image of prostitution in verse 25 is the prophets' picture for idolatry: Israel was bound to the LORD as a wife to a husband.

The verb stirred up, ur, returns at the very end of Chronicles, where the LORD stirs up the spirit of Cyrus to send the exiles home. The God who sends his people away is the one who brings them back.
passages.later: A psalm says, ‘Some trust in chariots and others in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God’ (Psalm 20:7). At the end of Chronicles, ‘the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia’ (2 Chronicles 36:22).
passages.hard:
Are the huge numbers of warriors, animals and captives meant literally?

Verse 18 gives 44,760 warriors, and verse 21 lists 50,000 camels, 250,000 sheep, 2,000 donkeys and 100,000 captives. Numbers like these appear throughout the historical books, and readers take them in different ways. Some take them as exact counts. Others note that the Hebrew word usually translated thousand, eleph, can also mean a clan or a military unit, so that some large totals may first have counted units rather than individuals. Still others think some numbers were rounded or enlarged in the telling to express the scale of God's victory. Each view has defenders among scholars who take Scripture seriously. The chapter's point does not depend on settling it: the eastern tribes won because God helped them, and later lost everything because they left him.

The chapter reports war and captives in the language of ancient records. It gives no one a warrant for war in God's name today.
passages.asks: The same tribes cried out to God in one generation and forgot him in another. Ask what in your life has drifted from trust to forgetting. And ask what it would mean to cry out to God now, before the battle.
